title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: A Mill, a River, and Destinies Colliding

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over this series we're going deep into one of the great novels of the nineteenth century — George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss.
A novel about a river, a family, and a young woman who contains more life than the world around her knows what to do with.
Joining me today are three people who know this book with the kind of intimacy that only comes from returning to it, again and again, across a lifetime.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher with a forensic eye for how fiction is made — the architecture of prose, the weight of a single image, the cunning of a narrator.
She's the person who will show us the machinery behind the magic.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels in audiobook form than perhaps anyone alive.
He hears the rhythms of a sentence the way a musician hears a phrase — and he will make sure we listen to this novel as well as read it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read The Mill on the Floss as a teenager and has never quite recovered.
She brings us the reader's eye — what strikes, what wounds, what sends you back to the first page.
Now — The Mill on the Floss is, at its heart, a novel about two siblings: Maggie Tulliver and her brother Tom.
And from the very first pages, George Eliot is doing something remarkable — she's building a family portrait so precise, so psychologically alive, that it feels like memory rather than fiction.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because the narrator of this novel is doing something quite extraordinary, particularly when it comes to Tom.
Yes — and it's a technical feat that I find more astonishing each time I return to it.
Eliot's narrator is omniscient — but she uses that omniscience surgically, not indiscriminately.
With Tom, she performs this double movement: she lets him condemn himself through his own words, and then she steps in and explains exactly why he can't see what he's doing.
There's a passage that crystallises this perfectly.

"Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into other matters of an intangible kind; he was quite sure that his own motives as well as actions were good, else he would have had nothing to do with them."
That last clause is devastating — "else he would have had nothing to do with them."
Tom's moral certainty is entirely circular — and Eliot exposes that circularity with the most apparently neutral prose.
She doesn't rage at Tom. She simply illuminates him — which is far more damning.
And when you hear that passage read aloud, it has an almost comic rhythm — until the full weight of it lands.
Tom is, in many ways, a magnificent comic creation dressed in tragic clothing.
But where Eliot really puts the knife in is when she gives him his actual words.
Listen to what he says to Philip Wakem — this is Tom at full throttle:
"I'll thrash you; I'll hold you up to public scorn. Who wouldn't laugh at the idea of your turning lover to a fine girl?"
The cruelty there is not just in the threat — it's in the sneering aesthetic judgment.
"Who wouldn't laugh" — as if Tom is appealing to some imagined audience, like a barrister working the jury.
It's chilling — and Eliot writes it without a single authorial shudder. She trusts us to feel it.
What strikes me, re-reading this, is Maggie's position in that scene — she is present, she hears every word, and she is entirely silenced.
Eliot tells us she is "suffering in anticipation of what Philip was about to suffer."
Her empathy runs ahead of the event. She is already inside Philip's pain before it arrives.
And then there's that phrase — Tom's "terrible clutch on her conscience."

"Tom had his terrible clutch on her conscience and her deepest dread; she writhed under the demonstrable truth of the character he had given to her conduct, and yet her whole soul rebelled against it as unfair from its incompleteness."
"Writhed" — that's the word. Not flinched, not resisted. Writhed.
It's a word that belongs to physical pain — and Eliot is absolutely precise in choosing it.
That word "writhed" recurs — and it's worth noting, because Eliot is building a pattern across the novel.
Later, in a later confrontation, Eliot gives us almost the same formulation — but now she frames it as a quality of Tom's mind itself.
She writes:
"There was a terrible cutting truth in Tom's words,—that hard rind of truth which is discerned by unimaginative, unsympathetic minds."
"A hard rind of truth" — that image is doing so much work.
A rind is the outer surface — the truth without juice, without flesh, without nourishment.
Tom sees accurately but without sympathy — and that distinction, for Eliot, is everything.
A rind of truth — I want that on a coat of arms.
But seriously — this is Eliot doing something that takes real nerve as a writer.
She is asking us to hold two things at once: Tom is right, and Tom is wrong.
The truth he sees is real — but it's a partial truth weaponised by a man who has never once examined his own heart.
That's a morally sophisticated position, and she sustains it through the whole novel without flinching.
And what makes it unbearable — in the best possible sense — is watching Maggie try to hold that same double truth inside herself.
Later in the novel, when she's pulled between Stephen Guest and her loyalty to Lucy and Philip, Eliot gives us this extraordinary passage of internal war.
She writes that Maggie felt "as if all the worst evil in her had lain in ambush till now, and had suddenly started up full-armed, with hideous, overpowering strength."
"Full-armed" — the evil is not a temptation gently tugging at her sleeve.
It arrives like an army. It's been waiting.
And then comes what I think is one of the finest sentences in the entire novel.
"She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."
"The best organs of her soul" — faith and sympathy as bodily organs.
Eliot makes the spiritual physical, and the physical moral, in a single stroke.
That's the kind of sentence that stops you cold — and makes you put the book down, just to let it settle.
We'll have much more to say about Maggie's struggle — and about the narrator who watches over her with such ferocious tenderness.
Coming up — we turn to the world this novel inhabits: the provincial society of St. Ogg's, the Dodson aunts, and the particular texture of English middle-class life in the 1830s.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Weight of Intellect: Maggie's Hunger and Constraint

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, where we read George Eliot's great novel slowly and with the attention it deserves.
Today we're deep inside the character of Maggie Tulliver — her hunger, her imagination, and the ways the world contrains her at every turn.
Joining me are three readers who know this novel with remarkable intimacy.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for fictional architecture is second to none — she will show us how Eliot builds Maggie from the inside out.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than perhaps any living reader — he hears Eliot's prose as performance, and brings that theatrical instinct to bear on every paragraph.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager, has returned to it many times, and cares about what it feels like from the inside.
We begin with Maggie as a child — specifically with one of the most perfectly rendered moments of childhood fantasy in all of English fiction.
What strikes me first about the gypsy passage is that Eliot sets it up as a comic scene but never condescends to Maggie — not for a single sentence.
The narrator tells us Maggie's intentions were, as usual, on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
"Maggie's intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined."
That phrase — 'as usual' — does enormous work in two words.
It tells us this is not a one-off impulse but a pattern — Maggie perpetually exceeds the frame that Tom, and the world, has drawn around her.
The comedy arrives from the gap between the scale of the fantasy and the smallness of its occasion — Tom walked off with Lucy and now she's going to live with the gypsies forever.
But the tragedy is right there underneath: this child has no other escape route she can imagine.
And when you read it aloud, that rhythm of 'No! she would run away and go to the gypsies' — that exclamation point is doing real theatrical work.
Eliot writes the free indirect thought of an eight-year-old with tremendous fidelity to how indignation actually feels in a child.
Listen to the sentence that follows the resolution:
"Tom should never see her any more."
Five words. Absolute. Magnificent sulk.
And then she thinks of her father and decides to send him a letter by a small gypsy — the practical arrangements have already begun.
The comedy of that detail is enormous. She's eight, she's heartbroken, and she's already delegating her postal needs.
What I keep coming back to is how Eliot frames Maggie's knowledge — or rather, the peculiar shape of it.
There's a passage just after the gypsy scene that I find almost unbearably affectionate in its satire.
The narrator says of Maggie's mind:
"in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
That word 'travelling' — as if her mind is a country, a landscape with surprising topography.
She knows what 'polygamy' means. She has deduced that 'poly' means 'many.' She did this from a dictionary, aged eight, alone.
And she had absolutely no idea that gypsies were not well supplied with groceries.
That is a child who has been given books but not the world.
And Eliot names that condition precisely — 'the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.'
That phrase does the whole novel in seven words. Maggie sees with piercing clarity in some directions and cannot see at all in others.
And what I love structurally is that Eliot then immediately enacts this — the fantasy collapses, and the way it collapses is pure Maggie.
Within five minutes, the gypsies have become potential cannibals, and the fierce-eyed old man is possibly the Devil himself.
The passage reads:
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
'Gradual cooking.' The specificity is devastating and hilarious in equal measure.
Maggie's imagination is not casual — even her fears are systematic and thorough.
There's a line just after that I find almost impossible to read aloud without pausing.
Eliot writes that Maggie wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded, whether the Devil would know her thoughts.
"she wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded, whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts."
No theologian could have exceeded. That is the funniest theological joke in Victorian literature.
But it's also perfectly serious — this child genuinely cares about getting theology right even while sitting among potential cannibals.
That's Maggie Tulliver in a single sentence: the comedy and the urgency are completely inseparable.
And that brings us forward in the novel — to a different kind of intellectual encounter, one with a boy called Philip Wakem.
Caroline, you've written about this friendship with great care. What's happening when Maggie meets Philip?
Philip is the first person Maggie meets who matches her intellectually — and who sees her as she actually is rather than as a problem to be managed.
He asks her about Philoctetes — the lame hero of Greek tragedy — and there's this moment where Maggie forgets Philip entirely and disappears into thought.
Eliot writes that she 'continued to lean forward, resting on her arms... while her dark eyes got more and more fixed and vacant, as if she had quite forgotten Philip and his book.'
That 'as if she had quite forgotten' — it's both tender and slightly comic. She has forgotten him. He's sitting right there.
But Philip doesn't mind. He looks at her 'as if he were not at all sorry to be interrupted.' He wants to watch her think.
Nobody else in Maggie's world has ever wanted to watch her think. Tom wants her to stop.

And then Eliot gives us something structurally remarkable — Philip asks a question that is ostensibly about fraternal love but is really about his own deformity and his longing to be loved despite it.
He says, with devastating simplicity:
"Maggie, if you had had a brother like me, do you think you should have loved him as well as Tom?"
The grammar of that sentence — 'a brother like me' — is doing so much.
He can't ask 'could you love someone deformed' directly — no child can phrase it that way — so he routes the question through the hypothetical of brotherhood.
And yet the longing underneath it is completely transparent. Eliot trusts us to feel it without naming it.
And then Philip delivers the confession that I think is one of the most genuinely touching moments in the novel.
He tells her:
"I'm very fond of you, Maggie; I shall never forget you. And when I'm very unhappy, I shall always think of you, and wish I had a sister with dark eyes, just like yours."
When I read that aloud in the recording studio I had to stop.
'When I'm very unhappy' — he says it as though unhappiness is his expected future state. As if he has already accepted it.
And 'a sister with dark eyes, just like yours' — he can't say 'I wish you were my sister.' So he invents a hypothetical sister and makes her look like Maggie.
That is the longing of a child who has already learned to translate his desires into what can be safely spoken.
And Maggie's response is characteristic — she doesn't deflect or soften the moment. She acts.
She wonders how she can convince Philip that she could like him just as well, although he was crooked.
That word 'crooked' — it's the word a child would use, unsoftened, and Eliot lets it stand without euphemism.
And then she offers something simple and total:
"Should you like me to kiss you, as I do Tom? I will, if you like."
It is the most innocent and the most generous sentence in the chapter.
She's offering him the exact currency of affection she values most — what she gives Tom — and she's offering it freely, without being asked.
Maggie's capacity for love is always larger than the world will allow it to be. That is the novel in a sentence.
Maggie's hunger — for knowledge, for escape, for connection — running up always against the limits of what her world permits.
Thank you, all three, for a conversation that has done justice to one of the most extraordinary children in English fiction.
In our next segment, we turn to the pressures Maggie faces as she grows — and to the question of what the novel asks her to renounce.

segments.title: Ruin and Reckoning: Mr Tulliver's Fall

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, the podcast that takes George Eliot's great novel apart, passage by passage, to see how it works and why it endures.
Today's segment is called Ruin and Reckoning: Mr Tulliver's Fall.
We're watching a man drive himself, with magnificent stubbornness, toward catastrophe — and George Eliot makes us laugh and wince in equal measure.
With me today are three readers who know this novel intimately.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher with an almost forensic eye for how Eliot builds her effects at the level of the sentence.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels for audio than perhaps anyone alive, and he hears the rhythms in Eliot's prose that the rest of us miss.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite let it go.
Let's begin with Mr Tulliver himself — the honest miller who believes, with total sincerity, that the law is a kind of cockfight.
What Eliot does with Mr Tulliver is one of the great comic-tragic conjuring tricks in English fiction.
She gives him a worldview that is internally coherent — and absolutely wrong.
The passage on his legal philosophy is a perfect little capsule of that.
She sets it up so precisely:
"Mr Tulliver was a strictly honest man, and proud of being honest, but he considered that in law the ends of justice could only be achieved by employing a stronger knave to frustrate a weaker."
That "but" is doing enormous structural work.
His honesty and his cynicism are not in conflict inside his head — they coexist without friction.
And then she delivers the image that crystallises the whole thing.
"Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck and the strongest spurs."
The word "injured" is quietly devastating — he always sees himself as the injured party.
And what a cock-fight it is.
When you get to the passage about Wakem, the hated lawyer, you understand viscerally why Tulliver is doomed.
Eliot gives us his loathing in one extraordinary sentence.
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!"
That exclamation mark after "fellow" — it's practically a fist on the table.
Eliot slips into free indirect style here — we're hearing Tulliver's own voice inside the narration.
And the comic genius is that even while channelling his fury, she lets us see how completely outmatched he is.
He knows Wakem has more law on his side — the text says so directly — but he can't stop.
What I find unbearable — in the best way — is reading that passage and knowing what's coming.
Eliot tells us he has an "uncomfortable suspicion" that Wakem has the stronger legal argument.
And still he goes forward.
There's something almost Greek about it — the man who cannot be warned.
And then there's poor Mrs Tulliver, whose influence on the disaster is one of Eliot's most subtle ironies.
Her pleading against the lawsuit — the pleading that is meant to stop him — actually spurs him on.
Because whenever she disagrees with him, he sees the whole Dodson clan standing behind her.
That's such a sharp observation, Caroline, and Eliot signals it in the most elegant way.
She uses that marvellous feather image to describe Mrs Tulliver's contribution to the catastrophe.
"It might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
But then notice what she does next — she immediately qualifies it.
The blame lies with "the previous weight of feathers" — all the accumulated grievances that were already there.
It's a deeply compassionate move toward Mrs Tulliver — she refuses to make her the scapegoat.
And simultaneously it's a structural argument about causation — nothing has a single cause in this novel.
I want to bring in the schooling passage, because it does the same thing on a larger canvas.
Tulliver sending Tom to Mr Stelling is another act of confident ignorance — well-intentioned, completely misjudged.
And Eliot contextualises it in this wonderfully withering historical indictment.

"There was but one way of doing this; any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price?"
The mock-sympathy in "was it their fault" — it's almost Swiftian.
She's making a systemic argument about institutional corruption, and she does it with perfect deadpan.
The individual fools — Tulliver, Stelling — are caught in a machine of foolishness that was built long before they arrived.
And then the crash, when it comes, hits so hard precisely because we've been kept at this ironic distance.
Eliot suddenly drops the satire and gives us Maggie.
"Urged to fuller speech by Tom's freedom from apprehension" — that phrase alone is heartbreaking.
She speaks, the text says, as if the words would burst from her.
"Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and the land and everything; he will have nothing left."
Everything.
It's such a simple word, and it carries the entire weight of the novel's first movement.
All the comedy, all the satire — it was preparation for this.
Caroline's right that the tonal shift is the instrument.
We've been laughing — or at least smiling with a kind of appalled recognition — through the whole build-up.
The cock-fight metaphor, the feather and the camel — those are comic constructions.
But Eliot has been loading the emotional bill the whole time.
When it falls due, it falls with compound interest.
That compound interest — paid out in the ruin of a family, the loss of a mill, and the childhood of two children.
We'll be returning to the consequences of that fall as the episode continues.
For now — the comic architecture, the systemic critique, the sudden plunge into tragedy: this, it seems, is how George Eliot builds a catastrophe.

segments.title: Laughter Amid Crisis: Comedy and Complicity

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's deep currents — its grief, its moral complexity, its extraordinary heroine.
But George Eliot is also, let's not forget, frequently hilarious.
This segment is about comedy — how Eliot deploys it, what it costs, what it reveals.
And no one better to lead us through that terrain than Oliver Trevelyan, who has performed more classic novels than almost anyone alive — and who hears, before anything else, what's funny.
I think Eliot is a great comic writer in the tradition of Fielding and Austen — and that she doesn't always get credited for it.
The comedy is architectural — it's built into the narration itself, not just the characters.
Take Stelling — the Reverend Walter Stelling, Tom's schoolmaster.
Eliot introduces him with magnificent irony.

She tells us that he meant to rise by merit — and then adds, "clearly, since he had no interest beyond what might be promised by a problematic relationship to a great lawyer who had not yet become Lord Chancellor."
That word "problematic" is doing enormous work — it's the whole satirical programme in nine letters.
And then comes the killer line about his ambition and his debts.
"A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting."
"Naturally." That adverb is a wicked little dagger.
What I love about Stelling is that Eliot holds the satire so steady — she never breaks into open ridicule.
The narrator speaks in the language of the character's own self-justification — "success was certain," "an absurd procrastination of the fruits of success" — and lets that language indict itself.
That technique — free indirect discourse deployed for comic ends — is one of the great inventions of the Victorian novel.
And Eliot is its undisputed master when she wants to be wicked.
There's something else I want to pick up — because the comedy in this novel is never just satirical from on high.
Sometimes it's tender. Sometimes it's complicit.
That passage with young Tom and Bob by the water — Tom imagining his Noah's Ark.
He says, "When I'm a man, I shall make a boat with a wooden house on the top of it, like Noah's ark, and keep plenty to eat in it, — rabbits and things, — all ready."
And then he adds — and this is perfect — "And I'd take you in, if I saw you swimming," in the tone of a benevolent patron.
"Benevolent patron." He's nine years old.
That class consciousness is already fully formed in a child's fantasy about saving his friend from a flood.
The "benevolent patron" is what kills me every time — because Eliot means you to laugh and to wince at exactly the same moment.
Tom genuinely wants to save Bob. The generosity is real.
But the hierarchy is so deep in him that even his rescue fantasies are organized by rank.
That's the knife inside the comedy.
And look at how that same note — ambitious young men, small lodgings, large dreams — gets reprised later in the novel.
Tom is older now, starting his rise in commerce, and Eliot winks directly at the reader.

"A touch of human experience which I flatter myself will come home to the bosoms of not a few substantial or distinguished men who were once at an early stage of their rise in the world, and were cherishing very large hopes in very small lodgings."
That phrase — "I flatter myself" — is the narrator stepping out from behind the curtain with a smile.
She's pulling the reader in as a co-conspirator — you've been there, haven't you?
And it's bracketed by Maggie laughing and running away from Tom's temper — that laughing retreat.
Even in the middle of real domestic friction, Eliot gives Maggie — and the reader — that moment of delight.
The comedy here is protective in a way — it cushions what could be a sharper scene.
There's one moment in the novel where the comedy turns very cold — and it comes from Philip.
Philip confronting his father — Wakem — about the enmity between the families.
He says, "You know best what satisfaction you would have, beyond that of gratifying a ridiculous rancor worthy only of wandering savages."
"Wandering savages." It's withering — it's practically comedy in its contempt.
But unlike the Stelling satire, there's nothing cosy about it — there's real fury underneath.
Philip is a character whose wit is always edged with pain — and that line shows exactly why.
That's the range Eliot commands — from the warm absurdity of Stelling to the corrosive irony of Philip's challenge to his father.
All of it is comic in some sense — but the register shifts from delight to devastation.
And that is precisely what distinguishes a great comic writer from a merely funny one.
From Noah's Ark to wandering savages — Eliot's comedy spans extraordinary distances.
Coming up, we'll turn to the novel's emotional centre — the relationship between Maggie and Tom, and what it costs them both.

segments.title: The Breach: Sibling Conflict and Social Obligation

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've spent time with the Tulliver family at home, watching childhood's particular loyalties and injuries accumulate.
Now we turn to the forces — and the institutions — that begin to pull Tom and Maggie apart.

Tom is sent to school under the Reverend Stelling, Philip Wakem enters the picture, and Eliot begins her sustained, merciless examination of what education does — and fails to do — to a particular kind of mind.
With me to unpack all of this are three readers I admire enormously.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and teacher of creative writing who reads fiction as an architect reads a building — for structure, load-bearing choices, and hidden design.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than anyone alive and hears every sentence as a performer — for rhythm, comedy, and the precise weight of a pause.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has been rereading this novel since she was a teenager and brings to it a reader's fierce personal loyalty.
Eleanor, let's start with Mr. Stelling and his teaching method — or rather, his non-method.
What Eliot does with Stelling is one of the most elegant satirical moves in the novel.
She doesn't attack him directly — she just describes him with perfect fairness and lets the portrait condemn itself.
The beaver comparison is the key.
She sets up this image of Mr. Broderip's industrious beaver, faithfully building its dam in a London flat three flights up — no water, no stream, no possible purpose.
"Mr Stelling set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid into the mind of Tom Tulliver."
The word 'instilling' is doing quiet, devastating work there — not teaching, not opening, but pouring something into a vessel whether it fits or not.
And the phrase 'natural method' — it sounds like praise, but by this point in the passage it means the opposite: a reflex, an instinct with no intelligence behind it.

And the passage keeps going and gets even better — because Eliot then explains that Stelling held his educational convictions in the same way a Swiss hotel-keeper believes in the beauty of the scenery.
Which is to say: professionally, without feeling it, because tourists seem to like it.
That comparison is genuinely funny, and it lands because it's so unexpectedly precise.

When I read passages like this aloud, there's a rhythm to the accumulation — she lists Stelling's pieties one after another, religion, Aristotle, deaneries, Great Britain as the bulwark of Protestantism — and then just leaves them there like a row of stuffed birds.
He's not a villain.
That's what makes it so bleak.
What breaks my heart — and I've read this many times — is how quickly Tom gets condemned.
Stelling sets him down as 'a thoroughly stupid lad' almost immediately.
And yet Eliot gives us this list of things Tom can actually do — predict horses cantering behind him, throw a stone to the centre of a ripple, draw almost perfect squares freehand.
These are the skills of a boy completely alive to the physical world.
But Stelling's school has no frame for that kind of intelligence, and so it simply doesn't exist.
And Eliot frames that problem through this extraordinary riff on metaphor — which is itself a demonstration of the thing it's describing.
She addresses Aristotle directly — it's one of those moments where the narrator steps fully into the light.
Here's the passage:

"O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being 'the freshest modern' instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence, with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without metaphor."
She's lamenting that we can only describe things by saying they're something else — and the lament itself is made entirely of metaphors.
The form enacts the argument.
Can we talk about Philip Wakem, because that's where the social comedy becomes something more complicated?
Tom's first encounter with him is this wonderful piece of prejudice observed from the inside.
Tom suspects Philip of spitefulness, connects his deformity to his father's rascality — there's genuine cruelty in Tom's thinking, but Eliot won't let it be simple.
And then she gives us this gem:

"There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood of Mr Jacobs's academy, who was considered a very unamiable character, and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his unsatisfactory moral qualities."
'Public-spirited boys' — she's practically winking at us.
The cruelty of children encoded as civic virtue.
And yet within the same paragraph Tom is looking at Philip's face with genuine, dawning attention.
He notices the hair curling 'like a girl's' — which Tom finds pitiable — but he's looking, he's actually seeing.
Eliot is doing something very delicate: showing us Tom's limitations and his capacity in the same moment.
And that capacity is going to matter enormously when Philip speaks.
Philip's speech about the Greeks is one of my favourite small moments in the novel.
It's so precisely rendered — the way adolescent idealism and strategic showing-off are completely fused.
He says:

"I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death."
And then the narrator adds — in parentheses, which is perfect — that Philip was 'not without a wish to impress the well-made barbarian with a sense of his mental superiority.'
'Well-made barbarian.' That's Philip's view of Tom — and it's both scornful and faintly envious.
These two boys are going to need each other and resent each other in equal measure.
'Died a grand death' — Philip wants the full classical package, doesn't he.
The tragedies, the wisdom, the heroic end — and there's something unbearably poignant in it, because we know what Philip's actual life will hold.
But for now he's just a clever, lonely boy trying to out-dazzle someone who doesn't know he's being out-dazzled.
All of this — the bad schooling, the prejudice, the two boys circling each other — is preparation for what happens to the siblings.
And Eliot closes this whole movement of the novel with two sentences that I find almost unbearable to read.
Just two sentences — and they carry the full weight of everything that has come before.
"They had gone forth together into their life of sorrow, and they would never more see the sunshine undimmed by remembered cares.
They had entered the thorny wilderness, and the golden gates of their childhood had forever closed behind them."
'The golden gates of their childhood.' She doesn't soften it.
The gates are closed and they are closed forever.
The biblical register is unmistakable — the wilderness, the gates, the expulsion.
But what makes it devastating rather than merely elevated is that one word: 'together.'
They go into sorrow together.
Which means the breach between them is not yet final — but the childhood that made them one self is already gone.
'Together' — and yet already moving apart.
The tragic irony of those two sentences is that they frame the entire novel's long grief.
In our next segment, we'll follow that grief into the years of family ruin and ask what the novel makes of loyalty — and its cost.

segments.title: Technique and Truth: How Eliot Builds Moral Complexity

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been talking about the world of the Tullivers — their mill, their money troubles, their fierce family loyalties.
Now we turn to something more architectural: how George Eliot actually builds moral complexity on the page.
With me for this segment are three readers whose company I find invaluable whenever the novels get serious.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who treats fictional craft as a kind of detective work — she finds the hidden mechanism and shows you how it runs.
Oliver Trevelyan has lent his voice to more classic novels than almost anyone alive, and he hears the rhythms and timing of prose the way a musician hears a score.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite recovered — in the best possible way.
Eleanor, I want to start with you, because this novel opens in a way that is genuinely strange.
The narrator wakes up from a daydream and announces that the whole opening was a reverie.
What is Eliot doing there, structurally?
It's one of the most daring opening gambits in Victorian fiction, and it tends to sneak past readers who aren't watching closely.
Eliot has given us pages of vividly present-tense description — the mill, the river, the child — and then she simply pulls the rug away.
The narrator confesses, with almost comic abruptness:

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
That word — benumbed — is doing extraordinary work.
It's a physical sensation of numbness, yes, but it's also the narrator admitting to a kind of trance — a voluntary surrender to the past.
And by staging this as a waking from reverie, Eliot insists from the very first page that everything in this novel is mediated through memory — which is never innocent and never complete.
And as a performer, you feel that shift in the body — literally.
You've been reading with a certain warmth, a certain intimacy — this is the mill, this is the river, come with me — and then suddenly the narrator looks down at her own arms.
It deflates the grandeur beautifully.
But what strikes me is that it also immediately re-inflates it — because now you know you are in the hands of a narrator who is consciously dreaming this for you.
That intimacy of 'I have been dreaming' creates a kind of complicity between narrator and reader that the novel will trade on for hundreds of pages.
What moves me about that passage is the phrase 'many years ago.'
It's so quiet and so enormous at the same time.
You suddenly understand that everything you're about to read is already over.
The mill, the child, the river — they exist in that perfect amber of memory, already lost before the story has even properly begun.
And that sense of loss — of things not fully recoverable — becomes almost a structural principle for the whole novel.
There's a passage near the end that I keep coming back to, because it's almost a thesis statement for everything Eliot is doing.

"Nature repairs her ravages, but not all. The uptorn trees are not rooted again; the parted hills are left scarred; if there is a new growth, the trees are not the same as the old, and the hills underneath their green vesture bear the marks of the past rending."
And then she delivers the line that crystallises everything:
"To the eyes that have dwelt on the past, there is no thorough repair."
That phrase — 'the eyes that have dwelt on the past' — is so precise about the mechanism of grief.
It's not that loss is permanent in some abstract sense — it's that certain eyes, formed by certain experiences, can never stop seeing the scar beneath the green.
'Underneath their green vesture bear the marks of the past rending' — that's not prose, that's elegy.
When I read passages like that aloud, I always feel Eliot leaning on the Biblical cadence — 'green vesture,' 'past rending' — it has the weight of scripture without the doctrine.
And that means the secular grief carries a kind of sacred gravity.
Can we talk about how this applies to Maggie specifically?
Because I think Eliot performs the same double movement — comic observation shading into something devastating — when she writes about Maggie's childhood despair.
There's a passage where Maggie has run upstairs in tears, and the narrator offers this:
"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others."
'Superadded life' — that is such a strange and perfect coinage.
The idea that maturity gives you other people's lives to live alongside your own — and that the young have not yet accumulated that — it's philosophically exact and heartbreaking at once.
Yes — and notice the structure of that sentence: the main clause is devastating, but then comes the subordinate clause that turns the knife.
'Though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the future lightened the blind sufferer's present.'
Eliot implicates us — the adult readers who are watching Maggie — and exposes our comfortable condescension.
We think our hindsight is a gift we can extend to her, and she reminds us it isn't — it's ours, and it changes nothing for the child in the room.
This is where Eliot is doing something quite different from, say, a novelist who simply asks you to pity the protagonist.
She keeps catching you in a moral position you haven't chosen — and then examining it.
That same move happens with the extraordinary passage about Maggie and little Lucy Deane — which is one of the most honest things ever written about childhood jealousy.
The narrator observes:

"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her."
'A little white mouse' — the simile is doing something almost too clever to be decent.
It tells us Maggie's affection for Lucy was always a kind of proprietorial fondness — the fondness of the one who is doing the petting.
And the passage goes even further, which is where Eliot's courage really shows.
Maggie is 'actually beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom.'
Eliot gives us the ugliness without flinching and without condemnation.
She simply explains the mechanism — Tom preferred Lucy, therefore Lucy became part of his unkindness — and lets us recognise something true about ourselves.
That is the moral complexity Eleanor is talking about — not a lecture, but a mirror.
Exactly — and it connects back to that devastating line about 'the world outside the books was not a happy one, Maggie felt.'
Maggie has formed her moral expectations from fiction — from books full of tender, agreeable people.
And Eliot, writing a novel, is very aware that she is one of those books.
The question she's asking — of herself, as a novelist — is whether fiction can tell the truth about human want without simply feeding it more comfortable fantasies.
That idea — that the novel is aware of its own position in Maggie's psychology — feels like something we could spend an entire episode on.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — that was a remarkable exchange.
When we return, we'll be looking at the Tulliver world more closely — the provincial society that shapes and constrains everyone in it.

segments.title: Closing: The Flood and What It Means

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the currents that run beneath this novel — the passions, the frustrations, the family bonds that bind and sometimes break.
Before we close, I want to bring all three of you back to something that feels essential: the relationship between what Maggie feels and what she is actually able to do in the world.
Eleanor, there's a passage early in the novel that I think crystallises this entire problem in a single extraordinary sentence.
Yes — and it's one of those sentences where you realise Eliot is doing something almost impossibly ambitious.
She's writing comedy and tragedy at exactly the same moment, in the same breath.
The sentence begins in high tragic register — Maggie consumed by warring passions — and then it pivots on a Greek phrase.
"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only."
The Greek phrase she inserts — τι μέγεθος — means something like 'greatness of scale,' the Aristotelian quality that elevates suffering into tragedy.
And then — the payoff — this colossal tragic intensity collapses into Maggie pushing Lucy into the mud.
It's heartbreaking and hilarious simultaneously, and structurally it's a perfect miniature of the whole novel.
The phrase 'poor little pink-and-white Lucy' — I mean, that's doing so much work.
Lucy as a kind of decorative object, almost a china figurine, landed in the cow-trodden mud.
When I've read that passage aloud, the laughter from the audience arrives just a beat after they feel guilty for laughing.
Which is exactly the effect Eliot is after — she wants you slightly off-balance, never sure whether to smile or wince.
And it matters enormously that the action is so physically small — 'the utmost Maggie could do, with a fierce thrust of her small brown arm.'
The word 'utmost' is savage — this is Maggie at full stretch, and the world reduces it to slapstick.
What undoes me every time is that this is Maggie as a child.
The gap between her inner life and the world's capacity to receive it — that gap never closes.
And Eliot sees it from the very beginning, in this child pushing another child into the mud.
It connects so directly for me with those chapters at Stelling's — Tom praying for Latin, Maggie lost in the Latin Grammar.
There's that extraordinary image of her reading the fragmentary examples — Eliot writes that they were
"like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown plants, brought from some far-off region" — "gave boundless scope to her imagination."
She finds in this dry grammar book a whole undiscovered world.
Because that's what Maggie's mind does — it transforms whatever it touches into something vast.
And Tom beside her, praying — actually praying — to be let off Euclid.
The comedy there is so tender that it almost hurts.
He adds, in the same whisper as his prayers for his family, the petition:
"and please to make me always remember my Latin."
It's one of the most quietly devastating sentences in the book.
Tom, who we might dismiss as rigid and unimaginative, is revealed here to be entirely, painfully human.
And Eliot wants us to hold both children — the one lost in golden far-off regions and the one whispering to God about Latin conjugations — at the same time.
What I keep returning to is the sword scene — Tom and Maggie together, and Tom counting.
'One — two,' said Tom, resolutely, though at 'two' his wrist trembled a little.
That trembling wrist — it's everything Eliot wants us to know about Tom in a single physical detail.
He's performing courage for his little sister, and his body tells the truth his pride won't allow.
And then when he falls and Maggie thinks he's dead — she shakes him, this unconscious child, trying to shake him back to life.
And then the line that follows — quiet, almost plain — which says everything:
"She couldn't sorrow yet that he had hurt his foot; it seemed as if all happiness lay in his being alive."
That 'yet' — that single word — contains an entire novel of complicated love.
The word 'yet' is the whole of it, isn't it.
She will sorrow — the foot, the grievances, the lifelong friction between them.
But in this moment — pure, unqualified joy that he's alive.
That is the feeling the flood at the end of the novel calls back.
The book builds to that ending — to Maggie holding Tom in the water — by making us feel exactly this, long before we know we'll need to remember it.
That's a beautiful place to arrive.
A novel that plants its endings in its beginnings — that asks you to carry the childhood scenes forward into the grief that follows.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — it has been a genuine pleasure to think through this extraordinary book in your company.
And to our listeners — if this episode sends you back to The Mill on the Floss, or to it for the first time, we've done our work.
The text rewards every return.

c37:p64.text:
Not a word was spoken as they walked along. Maggie was suffering in
anticipation of what Philip was about to suffer, and dreading the galling words
that would fall on him from Tom’s lips; but she felt it was in vain to
attempt anything but submission. Tom had his terrible clutch on her conscience
and her deepest dread; she writhed under the demonstrable truth of the
character he had given to her conduct, and yet her whole soul rebelled against
it as unfair from its incompleteness. He, meanwhile, felt the impetus of his
indignation diverted toward Philip. He did not know how much of an old boyish
repulsion and of mere personal pride and animosity was concerned in the bitter
severity of the words by which he meant to do the duty of a son and a brother.
Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into
other matters of an intangible kind; he was quite sure that his own motives as
well as actions were good, else he would have had nothing to do with them.
c37:p64.summary: Maggie suffers in anticipation of Philip's suffering and Tom's cruel words; she feels Tom's moral leverage over her conscience but rebels against his characterisation as incomplete and unfair. Tom, unaware of his own boyish repulsion and personal pride underlying his severity, is convinced his motives are good because he would not otherwise engage in them.
c37:p64.best_quote: Tom had his terrible clutch on her conscience and her deepest dread; she writhed under the demonstrable truth of the character he had given to her conduct, and yet her whole soul rebelled against it as unfair from its incompleteness. He, meanwhile, felt the impetus of his indignation diverted toward Philip. He did not know how much of an old boyish repulsion and of mere personal pride and animosity was concerned in the bitter severity of the words by which he meant to do the duty of a son and a brother. Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into other matters of an intangible kind; he was quite sure that his own motives as well as actions were good, else he would have had nothing to do with them.

c37:p72.text:
“I should be very sorry to understand your feelings,” said Tom,
with scorching contempt. “What I wish is that you should understand
 me ,—that I shall take care of  my  sister, and that if you
dare to make the least attempt to come near her, or to write to her, or to keep
the slightest hold on her mind, your puny, miserable body, that ought to have
put some modesty into your mind, shall not protect you. I’ll thrash you;
I’ll hold you up to public scorn. Who wouldn’t laugh at the idea of
 your  turning lover to a fine girl?”
c37:p72.summary: Tom declares he will thrash Philip and expose him to public ridicule, questioning who could laugh at a deformed man attempting to court a beautiful girl; his tone is contemptuous and threatening.
c37:p72.best_quote: I'll thrash you; I'll hold you up to public scorn. Who wouldn't laugh at the idea of your turning lover to a fine girl?

c43:p37.text:
There was a terrible cutting truth in Tom’s words,—that hard rind
of truth which is discerned by unimaginative, unsympathetic minds. Maggie
always writhed under this judgment of Tom’s; she rebelled and was
humiliated in the same moment; it seemed as if he held a glass before her to
show her her own folly and weakness, as if he were a prophetic voice predicting
her future fallings; and yet, all the while, she judged him in return; she said
inwardly that he was narrow and unjust, that he was below feeling those mental
needs which were often the source of the wrong-doing or absurdity that made her
life a planless riddle to him.
c43:p37.summary: The narrator explains that Tom's harsh judgment, though containing painful truth, reveals his unimaginative nature; Maggie is trapped between defending herself and acknowledging his accuracy.
c43:p37.best_quote: There was a terrible cutting truth in Tom's words,—that hard rind of truth which is discerned by unimaginative, unsympathetic minds.

c52:p2.text:
Maggie, all this time, moved about with a quiescence and even torpor of manner,
so contrasted with her usual fitful brightness and ardor, that Lucy would have
had to seek some other cause for such a change, if she had not been convinced
that the position in which Maggie stood between Philip and her brother, and the
prospect of her self-imposed wearisome banishment, were quite enough to account
for a large amount of depression. But under this torpor there was a fierce
battle of emotions, such as Maggie in all her life of struggle had never known
or foreboded; it seemed to her as if all the worst evil in her had lain in
ambush till now, and had suddenly started up full-armed, with hideous,
overpowering strength! There were moments in which a cruel selfishness seemed
to be getting possession of her; why should not Lucy, why should not Philip,
suffer?  She  had had to suffer through many years of her life; and who
had renounced anything for her? And when something like that fulness of
existence—love, wealth, ease, refinement, all that her nature
craved—was brought within her reach, why was she to forego it, that
another might have it,—another, who perhaps needed it less? But amidst
all this new passionate tumult there were the old voices making themselves
heard with rising power, till, from time to time, the tumult seemed quelled.
 Was  that existence which tempted her the full existence she dreamed?
Where, then, would be all the memories of early striving; all the deep pity for
another’s pain, which had been nurtured in her through years of affection
and hardship; all the divine presentiment of something higher than mere
personal enjoyment, which had made the sacredness of life? She might as well
hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in
which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs
of her soul. And then, if pain were so hard to  her , what was it to
others? “Ah, God! preserve me from inflicting—give me strength to
bear it.” How had she sunk into this struggle with a temptation that she
would once have thought herself as secure from as from deliberate crime? When
was that first hateful moment in which she had been conscious of a feeling that
clashed with her truth, affection, and gratitude, and had not shaken it from
her with horror, as if it had been a loathsome thing? And yet, since this
strange, sweet, subduing influence did not, should not, conquer
her,—since it was to remain simply her own suffering,—her mind was
meeting Stephen’s in that thought of his, that they might still snatch
moments of mute confession before the parting came. For was not he suffering
too? She saw it daily—saw it in the sickened look of fatigue with which,
as soon as he was not compelled to exert himself, he relapsed into indifference
toward everything but the possibility of watching her. Could she refuse
sometimes to answer that beseeching look which she felt to be following her
like a low murmur of love and pain? She refused it less and less, till at last
the evening for them both was sometimes made of a moment’s mutual gaze;
they thought of it till it came, and when it had come, they thought of nothing
else.
c52:p2.summary: Maggie experiences an unprecedented internal battle between cruel selfish impulses and her moral conscience, as the narrator reveals her struggle between personal happiness and loyalty to Lucy and Philip through a passage of intense philosophical introspection.
c52:p2.best_quote: "She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."

c11:p0.text:
Maggie’s intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away,
was not so simple as that of going home. No! she would run away and go to the
gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more. That was by no means a new idea
to Maggie; she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and “half
wild,” that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of
escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances, would be
to live in a little brown tent on the commons; the gypsies, she considered,
would gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior
knowledge. She had once mentioned her views on this point to Tom and suggested
that he should stain his face brown, and they should run away together; but Tom
rejected the scheme with contempt, observing that gypsies were thieves, and
hardly got anything to eat and had nothing to drive but a donkey. To-day
however, Maggie thought her misery had reached a pitch at which gypsydom was
her refuge, and she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense
that this was a great crisis in her life; she would run straight away till she
came to Dunlow Common, where there would certainly be gypsies; and cruel Tom,
and the rest of her relations who found fault with her, should never see her
any more. She thought of her father as she ran along, but she reconciled
herself to the idea of parting with him, by determining that she would secretly
send him a letter by a small gypsy, who would run away without telling where
she was, and just let him know that she was well and happy, and always loved
him very much.
c11:p0.summary: Maggie resolves to run away to the gypsies after Tom's rejection, a fantasy she has long harboured as a way to escape family reproach and find harmony with her perceived wild nature.
c11:p0.best_quote: No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more.

c11:p34.text:
Maggie Tulliver, you perceive, was by no means that well trained, well-informed
young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days;
she had only been to school a year at St Ogg’s, and had so few books
that she sometimes read the dictionary; so that in travelling over her small
mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected
knowledge. She could have informed you that there was such a word as
“polygamy,” and being also acquainted with
“polysyllable,” she had deduced the conclusion that
“poly” mean “many”; but she had had no idea that
gypsies were not well supplied with groceries, and her thoughts generally were
the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.
c11:p34.summary: The narrator reflects on Maggie's unusual, self-taught education: sophisticated in etymology and moral philosophy but naive about practical realities.
c11:p34.best_quote: in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge.

c11:p35.text:
Her ideas about the gypsies had undergone a rapid modification in the last five
minutes. From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to
instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon
as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking; the suspicion crossed
her that the fierce-eyed old man was in fact the Devil, who might drop that
transparent disguise at any moment, and turn either into the grinning
blacksmith, or else a fiery-eyed monster with dragon’s wings. It was no
use trying to eat the stew, and yet the thing she most dreaded was to offend
the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them; and she
wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,
whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
c11:p35.summary: Maggie's fantasy collapses into paranoid horror as she imagines the gypsies as cannibals and the fierce-eyed man as the Devil.
c11:p35.best_quote: she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking.

c19:p18.text:
“It’s about Philoctetes, the lame man I was telling you of
yesterday,” he answered, resting his head on his hand, and looking at her
as if he were not at all sorry to be interrupted. Maggie, in her absent way,
continued to lean forward, resting on her arms and moving her feet about, while
her dark eyes got more and more fixed and vacant, as if she had quite forgotten
Philip and his book.
c19:p18.summary: Philip asks whether Maggie would love him as well as Tom if he were her brother, a question laden with the subtext of his physical deformity and desire for affection.
c19:p18.best_quote: Maggie, if you had had a brother like me, do you think you should have loved him as well as Tom?

c19:p27.text: “Oh, yes, I should think so,” said Maggie, laughing.
c19:p27.summary: Philip confesses his deep and enduring affection for Maggie, stating he will remember her always and, in unhappiness, will think of her and wish for a sister with her dark eyes.
c19:p27.best_quote: I'm very fond of you, Maggie; I shall never forget you. And when I'm very unhappy, I shall always think of you, and wish I had a sister with dark eyes, just like yours.

c19:p31.text:
“Why, I think you’re fonder of me than Tom is,” said Maggie,
rather sorrowfully. Then, wondering how she could convince Philip that she
could like him just as well, although he was crooked, she said:
c19:p31.summary: Wondering how to demonstrate that she can love Philip despite his deformity, Maggie offers to kiss him as she kisses her brother Tom.
c19:p31.best_quote: Should you like me to kiss you, as I do Tom? I will, if you like.

c15:p9.text:
Mr Tulliver was a strictly honest man, and proud of being honest, but he
considered that in law the ends of justice could only be achieved by employing
a stronger knave to frustrate a weaker. Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which
it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck
and the strongest spurs.
c15:p9.summary: The narrator explains Mr Tulliver's philosophy: he considers himself honest but believes justice in law requires employing a cleverer knave to defeat one's opponent.
c15:p9.best_quote: Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck and the strongest spurs

c15:p19.text:
But not even a direct argument from that typical Dodson female herself against
his going to law could have heightened his disposition toward it so much as the
mere thought of Wakem, continually freshened by the sight of the too able
attorney on market-days. Wakem, to his certain knowledge, was (metaphorically
speaking) at the bottom of Pivart’s irrigation; Wakem had tried to make
Dix stand out, and go to law about the dam; it was unquestionably Wakem who had
caused Mr Tulliver to lose the suit about the right of road and the bridge
that made a thoroughfare of his land for every vagabond who preferred an
opportunity of damaging private property to walking like an honest man along
the highroad; all lawyers were more or less rascals, but Wakem’s
rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in
opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver’s interests and
opinions. And as an extra touch of bitterness, the injured miller had recently,
in borrowing the five hundred pounds, been obliged to carry a little business
to Wakem’s office on his own account. A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool
as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game! And it was vexatious
that Lawyer Gore was not more like him, but was a bald, round-featured man,
with bland manners and fat hands; a game-cock that you would be rash to bet
upon against Wakem. Gore was a sly fellow. His weakness did not lie on the side
of scrupulosity; but the largest amount of winking, however significant, is not
equivalent to seeing through a stone wall; and confident as Mr Tulliver was in
his principle that water was water, and in the direct inference that Pivart had
not a leg to stand on in this affair of irrigation, he had an uncomfortable
suspicion that Wakem had more law to show against this (rationally)
irrefragable inference than Gore could show for it. But then, if they went to
law, there was a chance for Mr Tulliver to employ Counsellor Wylde on his
side, instead of having that admirable bully against him; and the prospect of
seeing a witness of Wakem’s made to perspire and become confounded, as
Mr Tulliver’s witness had once been, was alluring to the love of
retributive justice.
c15:p19.summary: The narrator details Mr Tulliver's bitter conviction that Wakem orchestrates all his legal troubles and has humiliated him repeatedly; reveals his visceral hatred of the lawyer.
c15:p19.best_quote: A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!

c15:p18.text:
Mrs Tulliver, as we have seen, was not without influence over her husband. No
woman is; she can always incline him to do either what she wishes, or the
reverse; and on the composite impulses that were threatening to hurry Mr
Tulliver into “law,” Mrs Tulliver’s monotonous pleading had
doubtless its share of force; it might even be comparable to that proverbial
feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel’s back;
though, on a strictly impartial view, the blame ought rather to lie with the
previous weight of feathers which had already placed the back in such imminent
peril that an otherwise innocent feather could not settle on it without
mischief. Not that Mrs Tulliver’s feeble beseeching could have had this
feather’s weight in virtue of her single personality; but whenever she
departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of
the Dodson family; and it was a guiding principle with Mr Tulliver to let the
Dodsons know that they were not to domineer over  him , or—more
specifically—that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female
Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.
c15:p18.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs Tulliver's weak pleading against law has cumulative force when combined with his fear of Dodson influence, though she is not powerful in herself.
c15:p18.best_quote: it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back

c17:p2.text:
All this, you remember, happened in those dark ages when there were no schools
of design; before schoolmasters were invariably men of scrupulous integrity,
and before the clergy were all men of enlarged minds and varied culture. In
those less favoured days, it is no fable that there were other clergymen
besides Mr Stelling who had narrow intellects and large wants, and whose
income, by a logical confusion to which Fortune, being a female as well as
blindfold, is peculiarly liable, was proportioned not to their wants but to
their intellect, with which income has clearly no inherent relation. The
problem these gentlemen had to solve was to readjust the proportion between
their wants and their income; and since wants are not easily starved to death,
the simpler method appeared to be to raise their income. There was but one way
of doing this; any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good
work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their
only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price? Besides, how
should Mr Stelling be expected to know that education was a delicate and
difficult business, any more than an animal endowed with a power of boring a
hole through a rock should be expected to have wide views of excavation? Mr
Stelling’s faculties had been early trained to boring in a straight line,
and he had no faculty to spare. But among Tom’s contemporaries, whose
fathers cast their sons on clerical instruction to find them ignorant after
many days, there were many far less lucky than Tom Tulliver. Education was
almost entirely a matter of luck—usually of ill-luck—in those
distant days. The state of mind in which you take a billiard-cue or a dice-box
in your hand is one of sober certainty compared with that of old-fashioned
fathers, like Mr Tulliver, when they selected a school or a tutor for their
sons. Excellent men, who had been forced all their lives to spell on an
impromptu-phonetic system, and having carried on a successful business in spite
of this disadvantage, had acquired money enough to give their sons a better
start in life than they had had themselves, must necessarily take their chance
as to the conscience and the competence of the schoolmaster whose circular fell
in their way, and appeared to promise so much more than they would ever have
thought of asking for, including the return of linen, fork, and spoon. It was
happy for them if some ambitious draper of their acquaintance had not brought
up his son to the Church, and if that young gentleman, at the age of
four-and-twenty, had not closed his college dissipations by an imprudent
marriage; otherwise, these innocent fathers, desirous of doing the best for
their offspring, could only escape the draper’s son by happening to be on
the foundation of a grammar-school as yet unvisited by commissioners, where two
or three boys could have, all to themselves, the advantages of a large and
lofty building, together with a head-master, toothless, dim-eyed and deaf,
whose erudite indistinctness and inattention were engrossed by them at the rate
of three hundred pounds a-head,—a ripe scholar, doubtless, when first
appointed; but all ripeness beneath the sun has a further stage less esteemed
in the market.
c17:p2.summary: Eliot reflects on the educational chaos of the pre-reform era, where incompetent clergymen like Mr Stelling ran schools as profit ventures, and anxious fathers had no reliable way to judge the quality of instruction their sons would receive.

c14:p2.text:
Mr Stelling was a well-sized, broad-chested man, not yet thirty, with flaxen
hair standing erect, and large lightish-gray eyes, which were always very wide
open; he had a sonorous bass voice, and an air of defiant self-confidence
inclining to brazenness. He had entered on his career with great vigor, and
intended to make a considerable impression on his fellow-men. The Rev. Walter
Stelling was not a man who would remain among the “inferior clergy”
all his life. He had a true British determination to push his way in the
world,—as a schoolmaster, in the first place, for there were capital
masterships of grammar-schools to be had, and Mr Stelling meant to have one of
them; but as a preacher also, for he meant always to preach in a striking
manner, so as to have his congregation swelled by admirers from neighbouring
parishes, and to produce a great sensation whenever he took occasional duty for
a brother clergyman of minor gifts. The style of preaching he had chosen was
the extemporaneous, which was held little short of the miraculous in rural
parishes like King’s Lorton. Some passages of Massillon and Bourdaloue,
which he knew by heart, were really very effective when rolled out in Mr
Stelling’s deepest tones; but as comparatively feeble appeals of his own
were delivered in the same loud and impressive manner, they were often thought
quite as striking by his hearers. Mr Stelling’s doctrine was of no
particular school; if anything, it had a tinge of evangelicalism, for that was
“the telling thing” just then in the diocese to which King’s
Lorton belonged. In short, Mr Stelling was a man who meant to rise in his
profession, and to rise by merit, clearly, since he had no interest beyond what
might be promised by a problematic relationship to a great lawyer who had not
yet become Lord Chancellor. A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions
naturally gets a little into debt at starting; it is not to be expected that he
will live in the meagre style of a man who means to be a poor curate all his
life; and if the few hundreds Mr Timpson advanced toward his daughter’s
fortune did not suffice for the purchase of handsome furniture, together with a
stock of wine, a grand piano, and the laying out of a superior flower-garden,
it followed in the most rigorous manner, either that these things must be
procured by some other means, or else that the Rev. Mr Stelling must go
without them, which last alternative would be an absurd procrastination of the
fruits of success, where success was certain. Mr Stelling was so broad-chested
and resolute that he felt equal to anything; he would become celebrated by
shaking the consciences of his hearers, and he would by and by edit a Greek
play, and invent several new readings. He had not yet selected the play, for
having been married little more than two years, his leisure time had been much
occupied with attentions to Mrs Stelling; but he had told that fine woman what
he meant to do some day, and she felt great confidence in her husband, as a man
who understood everything of that sort.
c14:p2.summary: Rev. Stelling is an ambitious, pretentious clergyman determined to rise in his profession through impressive preaching and scholarly pursuits, despite lacking genuine depth or means.
c14:p2.best_quote: A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting
